clue.text: Old man cracked nut

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so the words before it are smashed and rebuilt

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An elderly man has broken open a nut, or has himself gone a bit nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' suits nuts so well that it reads as plain description; it is the signal to rearrange OLD MAN into ALMOND.
explanation.definitionFit: The almond is an edible seed from a tree of the plum family, commonly sold and eaten as a nut.

clue.text: Charge boy in possession of source of opiate

indicators.note: someone in possession of a thing holds it, so the boy's letters wrap around the next piece
a source is where something starts, so only the opening letter of the following word is kept

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A young man is charged with possessing drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a police charge for possession; 'Charge' is in fact the definition, a quantity loaded at one time, as in loading a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is the amount put into something at once, such as powder in a gun or cargo in a vehicle, which is a load.

clue.text: Conservative's alma mater?

blocks.note: surface reading: the college a Tory politician attended
setter's reading: a traditionalist is called this phrase, and one's former school is literally this phrase too

explanation.walkthrough: Conservative here means a traditionalist rather than a party member; the phrase for such a person also describes, quite literally, the school you once went to.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of traditional, unchanging views is described with this idiom, and an alma mater is the former school or college someone attended.

clue.text: Editor standing on bed with puncture

indicators.note: in a down clue something standing is upright, read from the bottom up, so the abbreviation is turned over
in a down clue one piece placed on another sits above it, so the editor comes first

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for editor
a bunk is a narrow bed

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor stands on a bed that has a hole in it, perhaps an airbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puncture' looks like part of the scene, a punctured bed; it is the verb in the sense of deflating a claim.
explanation.definitionFit: To puncture a pretension or myth is to deflate it by exposing its falseness, which is to debunk it.

clue.text: Capital is managing to retain charm

indicators.note: the run of words keeps the answer held inside it, spread across the word breaks

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, starting after the C-A-P

explanation.surface: A capital city manages to keep its charm, like a tourist board boast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like a city to name, but it simply contributes letters to the run that hides the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A talisman is an object believed to bring luck or ward off harm, which is a charm or amulet.

clue.text: Blames lightener for destroying collection of classical sculptures

indicators.note: destroying a thing breaks it up, so the letters of the two words before are smashed and rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone blames a bleaching agent for damaging a set of ancient statues.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the real complaint that cleaning damaged these Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum.
explanation.definitionFit: These marble friezes and statues from the Parthenon in Athens, brought to London by Lord Elgin, form a famous group of ancient Greek sculpture.

clue.text: Bring down aircraft with setter's explosive device

blocks.note: to land an aircraft is to bring it down
the setter speaks of himself, so what is his is mine

explanation.surface: A setter boasts of shooting down a plane with his own bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring down' suggests shooting down, but here it is landing safely.
explanation.definitionFit: A landmine is a bomb buried in the ground that explodes when stepped on or driven over, an explosive device.

clue.text: Tease American about cause of obesity?

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the pair of words before it is read backwards

blocks.note: to rag someone is to tease them
abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: Teasing an American about what made them fat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: this is one widely blamed cause of weight gain, not the only one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet food and drink high in this carbohydrate is often blamed for excess weight, so it is presented as one cause of being overweight.

clue.text: Doctor uses a test involving new insight

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the following words are altered into a new order
something involving another thing includes it, so the rearranged letters take in one extra letter

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A physician runs a diagnostic test that brings fresh understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as a medic using a test; it is the verb meaning to tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: Astuteness is sharp perceptiveness, the ability to see accurately into situations, which is what insight means.

clue.text: Chap bled badly around opening of incision in jaw

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters of the word before are jumbled
the jumbled letters go around the next piece, holding it inside
an opening is the start, so only the first letter of the following word is used

blocks.note: a chap is a man
the fodder, taken letter for letter
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man bled heavily from a cut made in his jaw, a grim surgical scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In jaw' seems to say where the cut was; 'in' is only the link and 'jaw' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The mandible is the lower jawbone, the anatomical name for the bone forming the jaw.

clue.text: Invalidate points given to paying supporters

blocks.note: two compass points, north and east
the gate is the paying crowd at a sports match

explanation.surface: Points are awarded or cancelled in some dispute involving fans who paid to get in.
explanation.walkthrough: In British sport the gate is the number, or money, of spectators paying at the turnstiles.
explanation.definitionFit: To negate something is to nullify it or make it ineffective, cancelling its force, which is to invalidate it.

clue.text: Group of companies, not large, come for training

indicators.note: training shapes something into a new form, so the letters before are reshaped

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A small business group is invited to attend a training course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not large' reads as a description of the companies, but those words are part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A conglomerate is a corporation made up of several different businesses under one ownership, a group of companies.

clue.text: Send home Irishman entering Eritrea for revolution

indicators.note: one thing entering another goes inside it, so the man's name is placed within the country's name
a revolution overturns order, so the combined letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: Pat is a stock crossword Irishman, short for Patrick
the country name taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An Irishman goes to Eritrea to join an uprising and is sent back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' fits the political surface, but here it signals rearranging all the letters once the name is inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To repatriate a person is to return them to their country of origin, which is to send them home.

clue.text: Medic facing old ban

indicators.note: facing means standing in front of, so the medic comes first and the next piece follows

blocks.note: a vet is an animal doctor
standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A doctor confronts a long-standing prohibition.
explanation.definitionFit: A veto is an official refusal or prohibition of a proposal, which is a ban.

clue.text: Lacking in education, soldier returned to woman with books

indicators.note: something returned comes back the way it went, so the soldier's two letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier
a woman's name
New Testament, a collection of books

explanation.surface: An uneducated soldier comes home to a woman who owns books.
explanation.walkthrough: NT, the New Testament, is a crossword staple for books; any woman's name may be wanted, here a short one.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignorant person lacks knowledge or schooling, so the word describes someone who is uneducated or uninformed.

clue.text: Cook beast for English Sunday lunch?

blocks.note: to roast is a way to cook
beef can mean a bullock or cow kept for meat

explanation.surface: An instruction to cook an animal for the traditional weekend meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beast' as BEEF uses the older sense of beef as a cattle animal; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The roast joint of cattle meat with Yorkshire pudding is the classic English weekend family meal, so it exemplifies that lunch.

clue.text: Soup provided by conservative visiting scene of heavy fighting

indicators.note: a visitor comes to a place, so the abbreviation is joined to the place named next

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for conservative
the Somme, a First World War battlefield in France

explanation.surface: A Tory touring a First World War battlefield is served soup.
explanation.definitionFit: Consommé is a clear soup made from concentrated, clarified meat or fish stock.

clue.text: Everyone cutting shrub finds a place to dance

indicators.note: something cutting into another goes inside it, so the first word sits within the second

blocks.note: everyone is all
broom is a yellow-flowered shrub

explanation.surface: A group pruning a bush stumbles on a spot for dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' suits pruning a shrub, but here one word is inserted into the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballroom is a large hall designed for formal dancing, so it is a venue where people dance.

clue.text: A group of musicians plus  …

blocks.note: taken as written
the London Symphony Orchestra

explanation.surface: An orchestra and something more, with the ellipsis leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the sentence into 20 across, where the musicians are placed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean in addition or as well, joining an extra item onto what came before.

clue.text: Label derived from name of space occupied by horse

indicators.note: a space occupied by something has that thing inside it, so the animal goes within

blocks.note: an em is a printer's unit of space
a pony is a small horse

explanation.surface: A tag taken from the name of a paddock where a horse grazes.
explanation.walkthrough: An em, like an en, is a printer's measure of space, a common crossword source of two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An eponym is a term formed from a person's name, such as sandwich or cardigan, so it is a label taken from a name.

clue.text: …  where they may be found with choir part set out

indicators.note: things set out are laid in a new arrangement, so the letters before are reordered

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
also part of the fodder, doing double duty with the signal

explanation.surface: Continuing from 18 across: the musicians are found where a singing section is arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They' are the group of musicians from the previous clue, joined by the ellipsis, so the definition depends on 18 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre musicians playing for an opera or show sit in the sunken area before the stage, so that is where they are found.

clue.text: Washed down edges of spade in brickie's trough

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its outside letters, so only its first and last are kept
one thing in another sits inside it, so the kept letters go within the trough

blocks.note: a hod is the open box a bricklayer carries bricks or mortar in
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A builder's spade gets rinsed off in the mortar carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: A brickie is British slang for a bricklayer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hose something down is to wash it with a jet of water, so hosed means washed down.

clue.text: Daughter getting sick on herb

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for daughter
sick means ill

explanation.surface: A girl falls ill after eating some herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Dill is a feathery aromatic plant whose leaves and seeds are used in cooking, a culinary herb.

clue.text: Plant tree close to stream

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken

blocks.note: balsa is a tropical tree with very light wood
last letter of the word

explanation.surface: An instruction to plant a tree near a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as the verb for putting a tree in, but it is the noun defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsam is the name of several flowering garden plants, such as the busy Lizzie family, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Hang on to wife's regular underwear

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: to linger is to hang on or stay
second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone clings to a wife's everyday underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular' looks like it describes the underwear as everyday; it picks out alternate letters of the word before.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingerie is women's underwear and nightclothes, typically delicate and decorative.

clue.text: Tools used by seamstress finally unnecessary

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the preceding word is used

blocks.note: sewing tools
last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's tools are no longer needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something needless is not required and could be done without, the same as unnecessary.

clue.text: Drug runner carrying females' wrap

indicators.note: someone carrying something holds it, so the runner's word goes around the next piece

blocks.note: a mule is someone who smuggles drugs for others
F for female, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A drug courier conceals women's clothing among the goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete, but a drug runner is a smuggler.
explanation.definitionFit: To muffle is to wrap or cover something up, especially for warmth or to deaden sound.
